title: The bottle wall
body: Behind our science building there is a small greenhouse. One of its walls is made of bottles. Two winters ago the old wall broke. The school had no money for a new one, so the science club asked a question: could we build it from something people throw away? For three months students brought clear bottles from home. The club washed every one of them. The wall they built is not beautiful, but it works. Sunlight passes through the glass, and the plants inside stay warm even when the wind is cold. Visitors are often surprised when they hear the story, and the wall itself is surprising: nobody expects a wall to let in light. "We did not upcycle the bottles to save money," our teacher says. "We did it so that everyone could see what waste can become."

questions.q: Why did the science club build a wall from bottles?
options: Because bottles are stronger than bricks.
Because the school wanted a beautiful wall.
Because the old wall broke and there was no money for a new one.
Because the plants needed more water.
questions.explanation: 'Two winters ago the old wall broke. The school had no money for a new one, so the science club asked a question…'

questions.q: What is good about the bottle wall?
options: Sunlight passes through it and keeps the plants warm.
It is the most beautiful wall in the school.
It cost more than a normal wall.
It keeps all the light out.
questions.explanation: 'Sunlight passes through the glass, and the plants inside stay warm even when the wind is cold.'

questions.q: Why did the teacher say they built it?
options: To win a school prize.
To use up the old bottles quickly.
To save money for the science club.
So that everyone could see what waste can become.
questions.explanation: 'We did it so that everyone could see what waste can become.'

title: Two buses
body: Our school has two buses. Before last autumn, only one of them ran. Most families drove their children to the gate, and the road outside was full of cars every morning. A teacher who lives near the school counted the cars for one week. Then she showed the number to the parents at a meeting. Nobody argued. The school opened the second bus line the next month. Now the road is quieter, and the air near the gate is cleaner. Parents who once waited in their cars for twenty minutes get half an hour back each day. The buses do not solve everything. They still burn fuel, and their emissions do not disappear. But one bus takes the place of about thirty cars. Small numbers, our teacher says, are still numbers.

questions.q: What was the problem before last autumn?
options: The school had no bus at all.
Too many families drove to the school gate.
The road outside was closed.
The bus was always late.
questions.explanation: 'Most families drove their children to the gate, and the road outside was full of cars every morning.'

questions.q: What did the teacher do to change things?
options: She counted the cars and showed the number to the parents.
She asked the city to close the road.
She bought a new bus herself.
She wrote a letter to the newspaper.
questions.explanation: 'A teacher who lives near the school counted the cars for one week. Then she showed the number to the parents at a meeting.'

questions.q: What does the writer admit about the buses?
options: They are slower than cars.
They cost the school too much.
Parents do not like them.
They still burn fuel and produce emissions.
questions.explanation: 'They still burn fuel, and their emissions do not disappear.'

title: The repair table
body: On the last Friday of each month, a long table stands in our school hall. People bring things that do not work: a lamp, a school bag with a broken zip, a toy car. Three teachers and six students sit behind the table. They do not sell anything. They mend what people bring. The rule is simple: the owner stays and watches. If you do not watch, they will not mend it. "We are not a shop," the maths teacher says. "We are a class." Last month a boy brought a chair which his grandfather made. One leg was loose. The boy left with the chair and with a new skill. Nothing on that table is valuable. But the pile of broken things gets smaller every month, and the pile of people who can mend them gets larger.

questions.q: What happens at the long table?
options: People sell old things.
Students give away school bags.
Broken things are mended.
Teachers teach maths lessons.
questions.explanation: 'People bring things that do not work… They mend what people bring.'

questions.q: Why must the owner stay and watch?
options: Because the table is often busy.
Because the owner is meant to learn the skill.
Because the teachers need help.
Because things get lost easily.
questions.explanation: '"We are not a shop," the maths teacher says. "We are a class."' 与 'The boy left with the chair and with a new skill.'

questions.q: What does the last sentence mean?
options: More and more people are learning to mend things.
The table is getting longer each month.
Fewer people come to the hall now.
The school is buying fewer new things.
questions.explanation: 'the pile of broken things gets smaller every month, and the pile of people who can mend them gets larger.'

title: What the bin told us
body: Our class did a strange piece of homework in May. For one week we did not throw anything away. Everything went into a big box under the back window. On Friday we opened it. The result was surprising, and we were surprised. Half of the box was paper — old worksheets, printed on one side only. Nobody in the class planned to waste it. It simply happened, page by page. The next week we started a paper tray beside the printer. Any sheet with a clean back goes there. The tray is not an environmental plan. It is a shelf. But since May our class has printed far fewer new pages, and the box under the window has never been full again.

questions.q: What was the homework in May?
options: To count the paper in the printer.
To clean the classroom every day.
To write about the environment.
To keep everything they would normally throw away.
questions.explanation: 'For one week we did not throw anything away. Everything went into a big box under the back window.'

questions.q: What did the class find in the box?
options: Half of it was paper printed on one side only.
Most of it was plastic bottles.
It was almost empty.
It was full of old books.
questions.explanation: 'Half of the box was paper — old worksheets, printed on one side only.'

options: The class stopped using the printer.
The class prints far fewer new pages.
The box was moved to another room.
The school bought a new printer.
questions.explanation: 'since May our class has printed far fewer new pages, and the box under the window has never been full again.'
